turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Local research centre, good morning.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'd like to book a place for our team at the introductory data clinic. We have several questions about a service pilot, but we need to choose a manageable focus.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: What is the main subject you want to examine?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Waiting times. We also collected comments about satisfaction, but the immediate question concerns how long visitors waited before speaking to a member of staff.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: I'll record waiting times as the focus.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Thank you. We want to understand what our figures can support, rather than arrive with a preferred explanation and ask somebody to make the chart look as though it proves it.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: The clinic is available on the fourteenth of September.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: An earlier message from our coordinator mentioned the seventh.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: That was a proposed date before the teaching team confirmed its availability. The fourteenth is the date now offered.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: That works for us. I'll correct the shared calendar and ask our coordinator to replace the old message.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: We will send a confirmation with the final date.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll make sure everyone uses that version for travel arrangements. A date correction is only useful if the people affected can tell which message supersedes the earlier one, rather than treating two different dates as two separate opportunities to attend.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: What time does the clinic begin?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Nine twenty-five in the morning. The building opens at nine, but the teaching session starts at nine twenty-five.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: So we should arrive shortly before nine twenty-five and check in, rather than expect the clinic to begin when the doors open.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Exactly. The opening explanation establishes what the group will and won't do with its data.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll keep the arrival suggestion separate from the start time in our transport note.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Good. That helps avoid a situation in which one person thinks the appointment begins earlier simply because somebody else sensibly planned to leave a margin for finding the entrance.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: How many participants should we expect?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Seven people helped run the service pilot, but only five can attend the clinic. Please book five places.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Five places are available. Will those people represent the different parts of the pilot?

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Yes. We have someone from the desk team and someone who managed the records, so we should be able to explain how the information was collected.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: That will help. If the attendance changes, update the booking rather than simply bring a replacement without telling us.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll maintain one current list and collect questions from the two people who cannot come.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: What is the total fee for the five places?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: The introductory team booking is seventy-five pounds altogether.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Seventy-five is the full total, not the fee for each person?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Correct. It includes the materials used in the clinic. A later individual consultation would have separate arrangements, but that isn't part of this booking.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll give our budget holder the total and the scope together.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Please check the confirmation before paying. If it doesn't match what we've discussed, contact us to correct it rather than assume the difference represents extra analysis that somebody has requested on your behalf.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Should we bring all the original response sheets?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: For this introduction, bring a summary of the data and a description of how it was collected. We don't need the original records containing visitors' personal details.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll prepare the summary with the totals, definitions and any missing periods clearly marked.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Good. A summary that preserves uncertainty is more useful than a complete-looking table whose gaps have been filled with guesses.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: We'll also note which version of the service was running during each session.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: That context matters. Without it, two columns can appear directly comparable even when they describe observations made under quite different arrangements.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Will the clinic establish whether our new appointment system caused the shorter waits?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: It will help you examine that question and identify what the design can support. It cannot guarantee a causal answer from any set of figures.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: That's what we need. Several things changed during the pilot, and I'd like the team to understand why that matters.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: The leader will work through comparisons and competing explanations. Sometimes the useful outcome is a clearer descriptive result and a better question for the next stage.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: We'll present it to our colleagues that way, rather than promise that one session will turn an uncertain pilot into definitive proof.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Can we include material from another organisation for comparison?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Only if you have permission to use it for this purpose and can explain what the figures mean. A table with a similar title may still measure a different period or use a different definition.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: We'll check the arrangements and bring the source description alongside any permitted example.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Good. The clinic doesn't create new permission to share somebody else's material.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: We'll avoid copying a private spreadsheet simply because the other organisation's results look useful.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: A well-described public or permitted comparison can help, but an unexplained number from an uncertain source may create more confusion than insight.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: One participant needs information in a format that works with their reading software. Should we discuss that before attending?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Yes. Explain the practical format requirement in your reply to the confirmation, and we will check what the team can provide.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: We shouldn't assume that a photograph of a worksheet is equivalent to an accessible digital file.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Exactly. Tell us what is needed, and we can discuss available formats and any limits.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll ask the participant to describe the requirement rather than make the request on the basis of my own guess.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: That will give us a clearer basis for preparing an arrangement that actually helps.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: How should we report a change to the booking?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: Reply to the confirmation and include its reference number. If the session is very close and the change is urgent, use the contact number in the same message.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: Is a note in the public programme comments enough?

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: No. That doesn't update the clinic's attendance record.

turns.speaker: Organiser
turns.text: I'll keep the confirmation in our shared folder and nominate one person to handle changes.

turns.speaker: Receptionist
turns.text: That should prevent conflicting messages. A single current record helps the team prepare the correct number of places and understand which data question your group intends to bring to the session.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: Welcome to the research centre. The diagram places north at the top and the entrance on the southern edge. The hall in the centre is our reference point, with eight lettered spaces around it. Reception is directly south of the hall, in line with the entrance. It isn't in either southern corner. Please check in there before taking your materials to a teaching room. Staff will confirm the group and any practical update. A room that was used for a previous clinic may have another purpose today, so use the current arrangement rather than following a remembered route simply because the event title sounds familiar.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The methods room is directly north of the hall. It occupies the northern central position between the two northern corners. Today's data clinic begins there. An earlier plan placed the introduction in the north-west room, but the larger shared display is now available in the northern central room. We start with the question and method before examining individual charts. Please wait for the leader before connecting equipment or rearranging tables. If the teaching setup needs adjustment for your group, raise that at the start. A deliberate change can usually be explained and accommodated more easily than several uncoordinated changes made while the explanation is already underway.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The dataset desk is in the south-west area. It is west of reception and directly south of the space to the west of the hall. You can collect the prepared practice data there after the opening explanation. The examples are fictional and supplied for the learning activity; they are not a report of a real organisation's performance. Check the version label on your sheet, because different exercises use different definitions. If you compare columns from two versions without noticing that difference, you can produce a convincing-looking result that doesn't answer the intended question. The desk helper can identify the correct sheet but won't choose your interpretation of the exercise for you.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The discussion room is in the north-east corner, directly east of the methods room. The two rooms are on the same northern row, so the discussion room is not north-east of the methods room itself. It is directly north of the space to the east of the hall. Small groups use it to compare explanations after examining the data. A discussion should keep the observed pattern separate from the claim about its cause. The room isn't a place where the group must reach agreement at any cost. A clearly described unresolved difference can be more useful than a single conclusion that hides the reasons some participants remain unconvinced.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The checkout desk is directly west of the hall, level with its centre. It is north of the dataset desk in the south-west area, not in the north-west corner. Return the reusable materials there and tell the helper if a sheet contained an unclear instruction. Please distinguish an instruction problem from a result you found surprising. The first may require revision of the exercise, while the second may be exactly the kind of issue the exercise was designed to explore. At checkout, keep your own notes but return any shared reference cards through the stated process so the next group receives a complete set rather than a collection assembled from whatever remains on the tables.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The clinic distinguishes a description from a causal explanation. A description reports what was observed under the stated method, such as a shorter recorded wait in one session. A causal explanation claims that a particular change produced that difference. The second claim usually needs more reasoning than the first, especially when staffing, visitor numbers or procedures also changed. You can report a useful descriptive result without pretending the causal question has been settled. During discussion, identify which type of claim a sentence makes. This often reveals why two people appear to disagree: one may be describing a pattern while the other is judging a stronger explanation that the pattern alone does not establish.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: A comparison should use definitions that are sufficiently consistent for the question. One team may measure waiting from arrival at the building, while another begins the clock only when a visitor joins the desk queue. Those figures cannot be treated as the same measurement merely because both columns are labelled waiting time. The clinic asks you to inspect the definition before calculating a difference. If the definitions cannot be aligned, you may need to keep the results separate or qualify the comparison. A precise calculation doesn't repair a mismatch in what the original numbers represent. The interpretation must begin with the observation process, not with the appearance of the completed spreadsheet.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: When a value is missing, preserve that distinction. An unrecorded wait is not automatically zero, and it is not automatically the longest wait in the session. Either substitution would turn uncertainty into a specific claim. The team can describe the missing records and examine how different reasonable treatments affect the result, but it should not silently choose the version that produces the preferred story. A pattern in the missingness may also deserve investigation. If records are often absent when the desk is busiest, the available figures may give an incomplete picture. That possibility is a reason to examine the process, not a licence to invent the absent observations.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: During group discussion, ask what evidence would distinguish competing explanations. If one person points to a new appointment rule and another points to extra staff, simply repeating the shorter waiting-time figure won't resolve the disagreement. The group needs to identify which observations bear on each explanation and what the pilot did not record. The next stage may require a different comparison or a more consistent record of conditions. This approach doesn't guarantee that every uncertainty can be removed immediately. It turns a disagreement into a question that can guide further work, instead of encouraging participants to treat confidence or repetition as substitutes for evidence.

turns.speaker: Research host
turns.text: The closing review asks you to record a supported finding, an unresolved explanation and a next step. These three entries should remain distinct. A proposed future comparison is not evidence already collected, and a plausible mechanism is not an observed result. The team should be able to explain why the next step addresses the uncertainty it has identified. You may also decide that a particular claim needs to be narrowed before any new data are gathered. That can be a valuable outcome of the clinic. A clearer account of what the current evidence supports is useful even when the group leaves with a longer list of questions than it expected.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You've analysed the two service sessions from last week. Today we'll decide what to include in the next pilot.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I propose adding a comparison venue that hasn't changed its appointment system.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: I'd keep the next stage at our current venue and improve the records first. Another venue may differ in ways we cannot examine properly.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could you describe it as exploratory?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: Yes, and I still support adding it.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: I understand the possible value, but I remain against it for the next pilot.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Eli supports the additional venue and Nora doesn't. The disagreement concerns the design you can manage, not whether comparisons can ever be useful.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should each session record staffing levels?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Yes. We can't interpret queue changes without knowing how many people were serving visitors.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I initially thought the rota would give us that information, but it doesn't show who was actually available during each observation period. I support a session record.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What level of detail do you need?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: The number of active service points and when it changes, not personal information about staff.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then both of you support recording the relevant staffing condition. Keep the definition clear so a person on a break isn't counted as available merely because their name appears on the planned rota.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Nora suggests extending the observation period.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: I support that. Our short sessions may have missed the busiest arrival period, and that could affect the comparison.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I would keep the same length for the next pilot so we can first check whether the revised definitions are workable.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could you extend only one session?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: That would provide additional context, although we would need to label the difference.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I still prefer consistent short sessions at this stage.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Then I continue to favour extending the period, but I won't describe it as a shared decision.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Your final report should preserve the difference between a proposal discussed and a procedure actually agreed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your earlier draft included visitors' full names.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I thought names would help match their comments to the timing record.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: I don't support collecting them for this exercise. A participant code can make the necessary connection.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I agree now. I'll remove the name field and use the code.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are there any remaining reasons you want full names on the analysis sheet?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: No. I'm withdrawing that requirement.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: We should still test that the code is transferred correctly between records.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. Avoiding unnecessary identifying information doesn't remove the need for a reliable link between the observations that belong together.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about using matched time windows at the two venues?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I support that. Comparing a morning rush at one venue with a quiet afternoon at another would introduce an obvious alternative explanation.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: If we add the second venue, I would first sample a wider range of periods rather than restrict both to one matched window.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: So your objection isn't that timing is irrelevant.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Correct. I want more context before choosing the window.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I still favour matching the periods for the next comparison.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then Eli supports the specific proposal and Nora doesn't, even though both recognise that the timing of observation matters.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should the report label descriptive findings separately from causal claims?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Definitely. We can state that a wait was shorter without saying the new rule caused the difference.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: I agree. My first draft moved too quickly from the chart to an explanation.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: How will you change it?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: Give the observation first, then discuss the explanations and the evidence each would need.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: And mark any recommendation as a next step rather than an effect already demonstrated.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: That is a shared decision. It should also make your disagreements easier for a reader to follow, because the reader can see whether you dispute the recorded pattern or the interpretation built on it.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two additional records have you definitely selected for each interval?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: First, the number of service points actually open. A scheduled staff total doesn't show whether every point was serving visitors at the time.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: Agreed. We'll note any change during the interval.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you collecting staff names on that sheet?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: No. Names aren't needed for the comparison.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: We also rejected asking for the price of each visitor's most recent purchase. That has no clear role in this question.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then active service points are the first selected record. Make sure the definition identifies availability for service rather than simply the physical presence of a desk.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: And the second selected record?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: Count arrivals during each observation interval. A shorter queue could partly reflect fewer people arriving, so we need that context.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Agreed. We'll define the observation boundary so we don't count the same arrival twice.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you also recording every visitor's full address?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: No. That's not one of the selected records.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: The pair is active service points and arrivals per interval.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Those records may help examine competing explanations, but they won't automatically isolate the effect of the appointment rule. Your report should explain what they add to the comparison and which uncertainty still remains after they are included.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two simultaneous changes limit the causal claim from last week's pilot?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: The desk layout changed. Visitors could see the waiting area more clearly in the second session, and that might affect how the queue formed.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: Yes. We should state it rather than describe the new appointment rule as the only change.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does using the same timing unit count as a limitation?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: No, that helps the comparison.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: And the records were available for both sessions, so missing an entire session isn't what happened.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. The first limitation is a real change in the setting, not a general warning that every small study must have unspecified problems.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second simultaneous change?

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: The appointment rule itself was introduced at the same time as the new layout. We changed two parts of the service together, so their separate effects can't be identified from this comparison alone.

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: Agreed. The two changes need to remain visible in the account.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What should you avoid saying?

turns.speaker: Nora
turns.text: That the shorter wait proves the layout worked, or that it proves the appointment rule worked independently.

turns.speaker: Eli
turns.text: We can report the combined change and plan a better comparison for the next stage.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The timer didn't fail and the service wasn't cancelled. Keep the limitations tied to the actual sequence of changes you are trying to interpret.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: This lecture follows a fictional team examining a change in a public service. The first stage defines the outcome. The outcome is the result the study will describe, such as a waiting period measured under a stated rule. It should not change halfway through the analysis simply because another available measure produces a stronger pattern. The team distinguishes the chosen result from a broader judgement about whether the whole service is successful. A shorter recorded wait may matter, but it doesn't by itself describe clarity of advice, fairness of access or every other relevant feature. Defining the outcome keeps the scope of the claim connected to the information the study actually collects.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage proposes a mechanism. A mechanism is an account of how the change might produce the outcome. For example, a revised information step could reduce repeated questions and leave staff more time for the next visitor. That account is a hypothesis to examine, not a result established merely by describing it clearly. The team asks what observations would be expected if the proposed process were operating. It also considers whether the same observations could arise for another reason. A plausible mechanism helps organise investigation, but it should not become a substitute for checking the relationship between the intervention, the intermediate actions and the recorded result.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage lists alternative explanations. These alternatives are competing accounts of the pattern, such as a change in demand, staffing or the composition of the visitor group. The team should identify plausible alternatives before becoming attached to one interpretation of the chart. It cannot investigate every imaginable possibility, so it explains which accounts are most relevant and what evidence is available about them. Leaving an alternative unresolved doesn't mean the observed result must be discarded. It means the causal claim needs to remain qualified. A useful analysis shows the reader why one explanation is favoured, which others remain possible and what a later study could do to distinguish them.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage constructs a timeline of changes and observations. The timeline is a chronological record that shows when the intervention began, when other conditions changed and when the outcome was measured. This helps prevent an event that happened later from being used to explain an earlier result. It also reveals periods in which several changes overlap. A neat before-and-after label can hide that complexity if the supposedly earlier period already included part of the new procedure. The team checks the dates and records uncertainty where necessary. The aim is a defensible sequence, not a simplified story in which the preferred cause always appears just before the desired effect.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage uses triangulation to compare different sources of evidence about the proposed process. Triangulation means examining how records, observations and relevant accounts relate to one another, rather than assuming that three sources automatically make a claim true. The sources may share the same weakness or reflect the same underlying record. If they disagree, the team investigates why instead of choosing the source that best supports its preferred conclusion. The value lies in the reasoning across sources and their limitations. A consistent account can strengthen an interpretation, but only when the team explains what each source actually contributes and avoids counting the same information several times under different labels.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Selection can influence a comparison when the groups being observed differ before the intervention. People who choose an appointment system may have different needs or schedules from people who arrive without one. A later difference in waiting time could therefore reflect more than the system itself. The team describes recruitment and participation rather than assuming equal group sizes imply comparable groups. Where relevant information is missing, the limitation remains visible. Selection is not a reason to abandon all local evaluation. It is a reason to examine who enters each comparison and to make the claim no broader than the design can support about those particular people and conditions.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Measurement can also change between periods. Staff may begin recording the end of a wait at a different point, or a new form may prompt more complete entries. An apparent improvement could partly reflect that measurement change rather than a change in the visitor's experience. The team checks definitions and procedures alongside the values in the table. If the earlier and later records cannot be made comparable, it should explain the mismatch instead of presenting their difference as an unqualified service effect. A consistent unit is helpful, but it isn't enough if the events that start or stop the measurement have changed. The meaning of the number depends on the process that produced it.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Interaction is another possibility when changes occur together. The effect of one change may depend on the presence of another, rather than the two contributions simply adding independently. A clearer layout might help visitors use a new appointment rule, while either change alone would have a different result. In a small pilot, the team may not have enough evidence to estimate those separate relationships. It can still identify interaction as a plausible question for the next stage. The important point is to avoid assuming independence merely because the report describes the changes in separate paragraphs. The organisation of a written explanation does not determine how the processes operate in practice.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: A causal comparison also involves a counterfactual: what would have happened without the change under otherwise relevant conditions. That alternative situation is not directly observed for the same people at the same moment. A study uses a comparison or model to reason about it, and the quality of that reasoning depends on assumptions that should be made explicit. The team should not treat a convenient comparison as a perfect copy of the unobserved alternative. It needs to explain the important similarities, differences and uncertainties. Thinking about the counterfactual can sharpen the question, even when a small local project cannot provide a definitive estimate of the effect it hopes to understand.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: At the stage review, the team plans a replication of the observation procedure in another suitable period. A replication repeats a defined method so the team can examine whether the broad pattern appears again under clearly described conditions. It is not simply another event with a similar title. The review specifies what should remain consistent, what may differ and how those differences will be recorded. Repeating the work cannot guarantee that the original causal interpretation is correct, but it can reveal whether the first pattern depended on an unusual circumstance. The next stage should therefore carry forward both a method worth testing and the unresolved alternatives that repetition alone may not eliminate.
